summary: This record covers the research families that turn a capture of a person into an avatar you can drive. They all reach the same shape: a parametric human model supplies the motion, and Gaussian splats supply the look. GaussianAvatars rigs each splat to a triangle of a morphable face model with a local frame and a displacement; SplattingAvatar embeds splats on a triangle mesh by barycentric coordinates and walks them across it during optimisation, which it says makes the result compatible with skeletal animation, blend shapes and mesh editing; ExAvatar drives a whole body from a phone video through the SMPL-X model of body, hands and face; Gaussian Head Avatar drives dynamic Gaussians from expression coefficients on a studio multi-camera dataset; Meta's Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars add learned radiance transfer so the face can be relit in real time on a tethered headset; and the 2026 work makes an avatar from a single photograph. For a standards audience the conclusion is uncomfortable. This is the most advanced avatar work in existence and none of it reaches an avatar format: no VRM, no glTF with skinning, no named skeleton, no named expressions. The 'rig' is the parameter vector of a body model that has to be licensed separately for research use, and the deliverable is a checkpoint. On top of that the two best-known implementations carry a non-commercial research licence and no licence at all respectively, so even the code cannot ship.

coverage.note: Each method carries a modified splat rasteriser, and one of them documents the modification as an edit to a header file to raise the channel count from three to thirty-two. That is the state of the art's build process, and it says a great deal about portability.
